lessons.bbp-basics:
**Bloodborne Pathogen Basics — OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030**

Bloodborne pathogens are microorganisms — viruses and bacteria — that are present in human blood and can cause disease when they enter another person's body. The three most significant bloodborne pathogens in the workplace are Hepatitis B (HBV), Hepatitis C (HCV), and the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV).

Hepatitis B is highly contagious and can survive outside the body on surfaces for up to seven days. Fortunately, a safe and effective vaccine series exists for HBV, and OSHA requires employers to offer it to all workers with occupational exposure at no cost. Hepatitis C is also highly prevalent and is the leading cause of liver transplants in the United States, though no vaccine currently exists. HIV attacks the immune system and can lead to AIDS, though medical advances have significantly extended the lives of people living with HIV.

Exposure to bloodborne pathogens can occur through contact with infected blood or other potentially infectious materials (OPIM), including certain body fluids. Common routes of workplace exposure include needlestick injuries, cuts from contaminated sharp objects, splashes to the eyes, nose, or mouth, and contact with broken or non-intact skin. Understanding what these pathogens are and how they spread is the first step in protecting yourself.
lessons.exposure-routes:
**How Bloodborne Pathogen Exposure Occurs — OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030**

Bloodborne pathogen exposure in the workplace does not occur only in hospitals or clinics. Any commercial or industrial facility may have situations where workers encounter blood or other potentially infectious materials — from first aid incidents involving injured coworkers, to maintenance work on contaminated equipment, to emergency response situations.

Exposure can occur through percutaneous injury — a needlestick or cut from a contaminated sharp object that punctures the skin. It can also occur through mucous membrane exposure, when blood or body fluid splashes into the eyes, nose, or mouth. Contact with non-intact skin — skin with cuts, rashes, abrasions, or dermatitis — is another recognized route. Even intact skin is considered at risk in some circumstances when contact is prolonged or involves large surface areas.

Other potentially infectious materials (OPIM) include certain body fluids such as saliva (in dental procedures), semen, vaginal secretions, cerebrospinal fluid, synovial fluid, and any body fluid visibly contaminated with blood. Workers should treat any unknown body fluid as potentially infectious. Recognizing the exposure routes helps workers understand when precautions are needed and how to apply them consistently.
lessons.exposure-control-plan:
**The Exposure Control Plan — OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030**

OSHA's Bloodborne Pathogens standard (29 CFR 1910.1030) requires employers to develop and implement a written Exposure Control Plan (ECP) for any workplace where employees may have occupational exposure to blood or other potentially infectious materials. The ECP is the cornerstone of the employer's bloodborne pathogen compliance program.

The plan must identify the job classifications and tasks in which occupational exposure occurs, describe the protective controls the employer will use, and specify procedures for evaluating exposure incidents. It must also outline how the employer will implement engineering controls, work practice controls, and personal protective equipment. Importantly, the ECP must be accessible to employees and their representatives during their shift.

The Exposure Control Plan must be reviewed and updated at least annually and whenever new or modified tasks create additional exposure risk. When reviewing the plan, employers must consider and implement safer medical devices and document that input was solicited from non-managerial employees involved in direct patient care or exposure-prone tasks. Knowing what your facility's ECP contains — and where to find it — is an important part of staying protected.
lessons.standard-precautions:
**Standard Precautions — OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030**

Standard Precautions is the approach that treats all human blood and specified body fluids as potentially infectious, regardless of the source. Under Standard Precautions, a worker does not rely on knowing whether a person is infected — every contact with blood is treated as a potential exposure risk. This approach is the foundation of bloodborne pathogen protection in all settings.

Key Standard Precautions practices include wearing appropriate PPE before any anticipated contact with blood or OPIM; washing hands immediately after removing gloves and after any skin contact with blood; never recapping used needles by hand; never eating, drinking, smoking, applying cosmetics, or handling contact lenses in areas where exposure may occur; and minimizing the creation of splashes or sprays when working with infectious materials.

Hand hygiene is one of the most critical elements of Standard Precautions. Hands must be washed with soap and water immediately after gloves are removed, even if the gloves appeared intact. When soap and water are not available, alcohol-based hand sanitizer may be used as a temporary measure, but hand washing with soap and water should follow as soon as possible. These practices, applied consistently, significantly reduce the risk of infection.
lessons.ppe-controls:
**Personal Protective Equipment and Engineering Controls — OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030**

Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) creates a barrier between the worker and potentially infectious materials. For bloodborne pathogen protection, PPE typically includes gloves, gowns or aprons, eye protection (safety glasses, goggles, or face shields), and face masks. Employers are required to provide appropriate PPE to workers with occupational exposure at no cost to the employee.

Gloves must be worn when there is any reasonably anticipated contact with blood, OPIM, mucous membranes, or non-intact skin, and when handling contaminated items or surfaces. Gloves should be replaced if torn, punctured, or visibly contaminated, and must be removed properly — peeling from the wrist to avoid contact with the outer surface — before touching clean surfaces. After glove removal, hands must be washed immediately.

Engineering controls are physical or mechanical safeguards designed to isolate or remove the hazard. These include sharps disposal containers, self-sheathing needles, needleless IV systems, and safety-engineered sharp devices. Engineering controls take priority over work practice controls and PPE because they eliminate or reduce exposure at the source, rather than relying solely on the worker's behavior. When engineering controls exist, they must be used.
lessons.housekeeping-waste:
**Housekeeping, Decontamination, and Waste Disposal — OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030**

Maintaining a clean work environment is a critical component of bloodborne pathogen protection. Work surfaces that may have been contaminated with blood or OPIM must be cleaned and decontaminated with an appropriate disinfectant after completing tasks, when surfaces are visibly contaminated, and at the end of each work shift. Contaminated equipment must be decontaminated before servicing or shipping unless decontamination is impossible, in which case the contamination must be labeled and communicated.

Regulated waste — items containing liquid or semi-liquid blood, contaminated sharps, and pathological waste — must be placed in closable, leak-proof containers that are labeled with the biohazard symbol or color-coded red. Sharps must be placed in closable, puncture-resistant, leak-proof containers immediately after use. Containers must not be overfilled and must be disposed of in accordance with applicable regulations.

Contaminated laundry must be handled as little as possible and with minimum agitation. It must be bagged or containerized at the location where it was used, and must not be sorted or rinsed there. Bags must be labeled with the biohazard symbol or color-coded unless the facility uses universal precautions and all laundry is treated as contaminated. Workers handling contaminated laundry must wear appropriate PPE.
lessons.exposure-response:
**Responding to a Bloodborne Pathogen Exposure Incident — OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030**

If a bloodborne pathogen exposure incident occurs — such as a needlestick, cut from a contaminated sharp, splash to the eyes or mouth, or contact with blood on broken skin — the response must be immediate. Delay in reporting reduces the effectiveness of post-exposure treatment options, some of which must begin within hours of exposure.

First, the exposure site should be washed thoroughly. Puncture wounds and cuts should be washed with soap and water. Splashes to the eyes, nose, or mouth should be flushed with water. The worker must then report the incident to a supervisor and seek a confidential medical evaluation as soon as possible. OSHA requires employers to make confidential medical evaluation and follow-up available to any employee who experiences an exposure incident.

The post-exposure evaluation includes documentation of the route and circumstances of exposure, identification and testing of the source individual (if feasible and legally permitted), testing of the exposed worker's blood (with consent), counseling, and evaluation of any reported illness. Prophylactic treatment for HBV and HIV may be available depending on the source and timing. All information gathered during a post-exposure evaluation is kept confidential. Workers should never hesitate to report an exposure incident — early response can make a significant difference in outcomes.
